transcript:
This message comes from Schwab.
Investing with Schwab is like a hike with endless trails.
Go solo with self-directed investing,
take stops along the way with trading,
or choose a guide with full service wealth management.
Whatever trails you take,
you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington,
I'm Lynda Kenyon.
Efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine continue,
even as the war has expanded beyond Ukraine's borders
into northern and eastern Europe, and more.
NPR's Charles Maines reports.
Now, we're also seeing action further afield.
Ukraine destroyed a Russian naval warship
docked in Libya in the Mediterranean.
Russia has its own shadow role,
providing intel to Iran and its war with the US.
And just this morning, South Korea said it scrambled jets
to chase away Russian sorties operating near its airspace.
So the spillover is real, and the map is wide.
That spillover is fueling concerns
that NATO nations could be drawn into the war
since the core principle of the alliance states
that an attack on one is an attack on all.
The next presidential election is still two years away,
but as NPR's Tamara Keith reports,
there are signs the campaign is already getting started.
Democratic and Republican politicians
are promoting new books and sharing thoughts
about lessons from the midterms
while playing coy about their presidential ambitions.
In no time, those pretenses will be dropped
as campaigns begin in earnest.
The Democratic National Committee has announced
its 2028 presidential debate schedule,
a dozen debates with as many as 20 candidates
allowed to qualify.
The first one is set for next June.
The Republican Party debate schedule won't be announced
until early next year after a contested election
for chair of the Republican National Committee.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Nearly two dozen states are suing to block a new rule
that would push some 80,000 people
out of federal subsidized housing,
including many children who are U.S. citizens.
NPR's Jennifer Ludden has the details.
Immigrants in the U.S. unlawfully
do not get federal rental aid,
but in 1997, Congress said they can live
with family members who do.
The Trump administration calls this a loophole
and argues it's not fair to American taxpayers,
especially given the high demand and long wait list
for a housing subsidy.
But 22 mostly Democratic-led states
say pushing out such families
goes against what Congress intended,
and they say it would leave many HUD residents homeless.
The new rule also requires HUD tenants
to verify their citizenship status with the federal database,
but the state's lawsuit says that database
has a documented record of errors.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
Members of Congress have responded
with swift bipartisan fury over the decision
by the NVIDIA Board of Directors
to reinstate Jensen Wong as CEO
at the behest of President Trump.
The chairman of the Senate Banking Committee,
Republican Tim Scott, says Wong will testify publicly
before the panel on December 3rd.
And Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren,
the incoming chair, says the Trump administration
needs to explain what role U.S. officials
played in Wong's reinstatement.
You're listening to NPR News.
Towns along the old Route 66
are celebrating its 100th birthday this month.
Tulsa, Oklahoma is marking the occasion in its own way,
supporting the restoration and creation of neon signs.
NPR's Jennifer Vanasko has the story.
Tulsa has a neon sign grant program.
It reimburses up to 50% of the costs
for new or restored signs along Route 66, up to $10,000.
The signs must be vintage or inspired by historic signs.
Joe Kestersen is the senior designer
for the Claude Neon Federal Sign Company based in Tulsa.
He's worked on many of those signs
and he says they helped draw tourists.
Kind of the mystique of Route 66 is, you know,
that's what you would have seen traveling as a child
with your parents across the country.
Though neon signs are now thought of with nostalgia,
they were once seen as modern
and signified a clean, safe place to stay or eat.
Jennifer Vanasko, NPR News, Tulsa.
Honda is recalling more than 810,000 vehicles.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
cites concerns over airbag inflators that could rupture.
The recall involves Honda Civics and CRVs
with model years 2012 to 2013,
as well as 2013 Honda Accords, Acura ILX and RDX vehicles.
Authorities say the vehicles have certain
Toccata front seat airbag inflators
that may rupture due to degradation of propellant.
Honda says long-term exposure to high heat and humidity
can cause that degradation.
I'm Lynda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.
Plus at plus.npr.org.
That's plus.npr.org.
